passage: Morning in a flat in Manchester. On the fridge hung Javier's sticker chart, a row of little stars. He brushed his teeth and called, "Done, Dad!" His father Emeka pressed a sticker into the first box. Javier drank his milk to the last drop, and got a second sticker. He carried his shoes across the hall and set them in the rack by the door, a third. Then he counted the whole chart with one finger. "Eight! Two more and we go to the park."

qa.q: Which three tasks earned Javier a sticker in the morning?
qa.a: He brushed his teeth, finished his milk and put his shoes in the rack.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling as he counted the stickers on the chart?
qa.a: He was excited and eager. He counted with one finger and said "Two more and we go to the park." 😊

qa.q: What else could Javier do so he remembers the steps without being reminded, and why?
qa.a: He could draw a small picture beside each box on the chart. Then he can check the steps himself, and Dad does not have to call them out.

qa.q: How does Emeka see the sticker chart?
qa.a: Emeka sees a routine that Javier follows on his own, with a clear goal in the park trip, so he needs to remind him less.

grounding: A child works through a sticker chart step by step, each finished task earns a sticker, and ten stickers lead to the park.

passage: Dinner was on the table in the sixth-floor flat, and Vijay stared at his bowl of spinach and beans. He tapped the spoon twice. "If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?" His father Suraj raised an eyebrow. "All of them?" "All. Even the green ones." "Then two stories." Vijay made a face at the first bite, ate steadily after that, and showed the empty bowl. Then he ran to pick two books from the shelf.

qa.q: How many stories did Vijay ask for?
qa.a: He asked for two stories tonight.

qa.q: What might Vijay be feeling as he looks at his bowl and makes his offer?
qa.a: He is probably a little reluctant about the spinach but eager for the second story, so he is willing to trade one for the other.

qa.q: What other approach could Vijay use to get the extra story, and why?
qa.a: He could ask for a smaller helping and finish that first. A goal that feels smaller is easier to reach, and he would still earn the story.

qa.q: How does Suraj see Vijay's offer?
qa.a: Suraj hears a clear deal and gets the vegetables eaten. He also sees his son planning instead of refusing.

grounding: A child bargains, offering to eat all the vegetables in return for two stories, so the deal is stated openly.

passage: I'm Gautam, and I live next door to Usha. Yesterday I was in her house while she played with blocks and dolls. Her mum said, "Playtime is over." Usha said out loud, "If I put my toys away, I get a sticker." Then she dropped the blocks in the box and set the dolls on the shelf, without any more reminders. I can't know all she was thinking. But she ran straight to the chart on the fridge and pressed her own sticker on it, and she was smiling.

qa.q: What did Usha say out loud when playtime was over?
qa.a: She said, "If I put my toys away, I get a sticker."

qa.q: How can Gautam tell that Usha wanted her sticker?
qa.a: She put the toys away straight after the words and then ran to the chart, smiling. That suggests she was pleased and eager to earn it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help Usha tidy up even without a sticker, and why?
qa.a: Her mum could set a short tidy-up song or timer. It makes the tidying itself a game, so it does not depend only on the prize.

qa.q: How might Usha's mum see the rule?
qa.a: Her mum probably finds it easier, since Usha starts tidying without being reminded again and again.

grounding: A child holds the rule that putting toys away earns a sticker and acts on it as soon as playtime ends, showing she understands the link.

passage: I'm Lalremsiami, and I sit next to Seema in class. On Monday she showed me her sticker chart. She had wished on the first star the night before for extra stickers, and she was sure they would be there by morning. On Tuesday she ran to check, and the chart looked just the same. She stood still, then said, "The star forgot." She did not put her shoes in the rack that morning, and that box stayed empty. I can't tell what she thought, but she looked confused.

qa.q: What did Seema wish for on the first star?
qa.a: She wished for extra stickers on her chart.

qa.q: What might Seema have been feeling when she saw the chart unchanged?
qa.a: She was probably disappointed and confused. She had trusted the wish, and she stood still and said "The star forgot."

qa.q: What could Seema try next time instead of only wishing, and why?
qa.a: She could do the routine tasks and then count the stickers with a grown-up. The stickers come from the tasks she finishes, not from the wish.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see what happened to Seema's chart?
qa.a: Lalremsiami is puzzled and a little worried. Lalremsiami saw that the empty shoe box came from the skipped task, not from the star.

grounding: A child wishes on the first star for extra stickers and expects them on the chart in the morning, trusting the wish more than the routine.

passage: The pressure cooker whistled and the rain drummed on the window. Divyansh sat on the kitchen floor staring at his sticker chart, where some boxes were filled and some were empty. He could not tell if the reward, a trip to the fair, was near or far. He frowned. Then he tugged his mother's sleeve. "Mamma, how many more stickers?" Usha turned down the gas, knelt beside him and pointed as they counted the empty boxes together. "One, two, three." "Three!" said Divyansh, and held up three fingers to the cat.

qa.q: How many stickers did Divyansh still need?
qa.a: He needed three more stickers, the three empty boxes.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling before he asked his mother about the stickers?
qa.a: He was unsure and puzzled about how far off the fair was, shown by his frown and staring at the chart.

qa.q: What else could Divyansh do to keep the goal in mind, and why?
qa.a: He could cross off one box each night. Then he can see the count shrink by himself and does not need to ask every time.

qa.q: How might Usha feel when Divyansh interrupts her cooking to ask?
qa.a: Usha is busy, but she turns down the gas and kneels to count with him. She probably feels glad that he wants to understand.

grounding: A child unsure how far off the reward is asks mother, who counts the remaining stickers with him, and the goal becomes concrete.

subtype: Approach: giving up after a miss [Pitfall]
passage: After the family came back from the wedding, Tenzin looked at the chart on the wall in the Delhi flat. Two days were blank, with no stickers. He peeled a corner of the paper. "The chart is finished," he said. "I missed." His father Nitin sat down beside him. "Missing two days is not the end of the chart." He took a fresh row, drew ten empty boxes, and wrote today's date at the start. "We count again from today." Tenzin looked at the boxes, then went to find his shoes.

qa.q: What did Tenzin say about the chart after two blank days?
qa.a: He said the chart was finished because he had missed.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling as he peeled the corner of the paper?
qa.a: He felt discouraged, as if the chart was already lost. He gave up right away instead of trying again.

qa.q: What could Tenzin try after missing a day the next time, and why?
qa.a: He could put a small mark on the blank day and carry on the next morning. Then one lapse is a gap in a row, not the end of the chart.

qa.q: How does Nitin see the two blank days?
qa.a: Nitin sees a small gap after a busy wedding. He wants Tenzin to keep trying, so he restarts the count.

grounding: After two missed days a child declares the chart finished and gives up, until a parent restarts the count.

passage: Note to Rashmi's mother, Thursday. Rashmi came to the playgroup with one shoe on. I did not point to where it might be. I asked, "What did you do first today?" She thought, then went step by step in order. First the bedroom, where she looked under the cot. Then the verandah. Then the front gate, where she had played with the swing. The shoe was behind the flowerpot there. She held it up and put it on herself. Going through her day in order helped more than running about. Manoj, playgroup teacher

qa.q: Where was Rashmi's missing shoe found?
qa.a: It was behind the flowerpot at the front gate.

qa.q: How was Rashmi feeling as she went from place to place?
qa.a: She seems calm and focused, working through her morning in order. The note says she went step by step instead of running about.

qa.q: What else could Rashmi do next time so the shoe does not go missing?
qa.a: She could put both shoes on the same spot each time after playing. Then the first place she looks is the right one.

qa.q: How might Rashmi's mother feel when she reads the note?
qa.a: She would probably feel reassured. She learns Rashmi managed to find it herself, with only one question from the teacher.

grounding: A child finds a lost shoe by going back through the day in order, bedroom, verandah and gate, which narrows the search.

passage: Tanuja was hopping on one foot by the door, already late for school. "Mummy, I can't find my shoe!" Her mother Gargi did not search the flat for her. "Where did you last have it?" Tanuja stopped hopping. She scrunched her forehead and thought. "I took them off... when I watered the plants." She ran to the balcony. The shoe was lying on its side beside the tulsi pot. "Found it!" she called. Gargi held out the other shoe, and Tanuja sat down to put both on.

qa.q: Where was Tanuja's shoe?
qa.a: It was on its side beside the tulsi pot on the balcony.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling as she hopped by the door?
qa.a: She was worried and hurried, since she was late for school and missing a shoe. Then she calmed once she began to think.

qa.q: What else could Tanuja try to find things faster next time, and why?
qa.a: She could put her shoes in the same spot every day. Then she would know exactly where to look.

qa.q: How does Gargi see Tanuja's search?
qa.a: Gargi sees a daughter who can find it herself with one question, so she does not need to search for her.

grounding: A child asks her mother for help with a lost shoe and the mother's question about where she last had it gives the search a structure.

passage: In a flat in Manila, Bao was on her hands and knees in the living room, one shoe on, one shoe missing. Lola Rosa watched from the kitchen door. "Okay," Bao whispered. "I am the shoe. I am little. I like dark places. Where would I go?" She crawled around the room, thinking like a shoe. Her eyes stopped at the sofa. "Under the sofa!" She lay flat on the rug, stretched out an arm, and pulled out the shoe with a puff of dust.

qa.q: Where did Bao find her missing shoe?
qa.a: She found it under the sofa.

qa.q: What was Bao thinking when she whispered "Where would I go?"
qa.a: She was trying to work out where the shoe would hide by pretending to be it. She was curious and playful as she searched.

qa.q: What other approach could Bao try if pretending does not work, and why?
qa.a: She could ask Lola Rosa where she last had the shoe. Going back over her day step by step would show her places she had forgotten.

qa.q: How might Lola Rosa feel while she watches Bao?
qa.a: Lola Rosa is probably amused and proud. She lets Bao work it out herself instead of searching for her.

grounding: A child pretends to be the missing shoe and asks where it would go, and the imagined journey brings up the idea of looking under the sofa.

passage: At the preschool, Ishita stood at the door with one shoe on and one sock. "My shoe ran away," she told Nilesh Sir. "It will come back when I wait here." He crouched down. "Would you like to look for it with me?" Ishita shook her head and sat on the mat by the door, watching the corridor. The other children played. Snack time passed. When her aunt came to pick her up, the shoe was still missing, and Ishita hobbled out with a shoe on only one foot.

qa.q: What did Ishita say had happened to her shoe?
qa.a: She said her shoe ran away and would come back when she waited.

qa.q: What might Ishita be feeling while she sits by the door waiting?
qa.a: She may be hopeful and a little anxious, trusting the shoe will return. She sat and watched the corridor instead of looking.

qa.q: What could Nilesh Sir try next, and why?
qa.a: He could ask where she last had the shoe and walk there with her. That gives the search steps, so waiting is not the only plan.

qa.q: How does Ishita's aunt see her leaving with one shoe?
qa.a: Her aunt is probably surprised and worried. Her aunt sees a child who missed play and snack and now has to hobble out.

grounding: A child insists the shoe ran away and waits at the door, so waiting replaces searching and the shoe stays missing.
